title: Multi-stage and reverse problems
prior_knowledge_summary: From 9702_t02_cm03_l07, students can solve one constant-acceleration interval using known, target and unwanted quantities.
From 9702_t02_cm03_l07, students can choose a horizontal positive direction, rearrange before substitution and check units and physical sense.
new_learning: Split a journey when acceleration changes.
Carry a boundary value from one stage into the next.
Work backward from a later state and compare valid solution routes.
not_yet_taught: Free fall and vertical sign conventions
learning_outcomes: Divide a straight-line journey into constant-acceleration stages and identify the shared boundary value.
Carry an intermediate velocity, displacement or time between stages with a consistent sign convention.
Work backward from a known final state and compare two valid equation routes.

inside_scope: Linked straight-line stages with constant acceleration within each stage
Forward and reverse use of the three registered equations
outside_scope: Acceleration that varies within a stage

visual_rules.style: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch with basic annotations, visible pencil texture and only essential labels.
visual_rules.reason: Six varied visuals show stage boundaries, carried values, reverse arrows, route comparison, a misconception and a final workflow.

evidence_basis.evidence_summary: Mapped evidence links one calculated quantity to a later calculation and uses endpoint conditions to work toward time, displacement or acceleration. Original horizontal contexts avoid untaught projectile and free-fall knowledge.
evidence_basis.canonical_audit: Checked both whole canonical question chains and mark schemes. The lesson reuses linked-result and endpoint reasoning in original horizontal contexts to remain inside scope.

blocks.title: One trip, two accelerations
body: A test cart accelerates for 4.0 s, then its motor changes setting and it slows for 3.0 s. Can one equation describe all 7.0 s? Predict before calculating.
The acceleration changes at the switch. One constant-acceleration equation cannot cover both stages. The switch is a boundary, but the cart does not teleport or suddenly lose its velocity.

figure.purpose: Make the change of model and continuous boundary velocity visible.
figure.brief: Teacher-sketch timeline of a cart, stage 1 then stage 2, with a clear switch and one shared boundary velocity symbol.
figure.alt_text: A cart journey split at a switch into two time intervals, with the velocity at the end of stage 1 also shown at the start of stage 2.

blocks.title: Build one snapshot per stage
body: Draw a separate u-v-a-s-t row for each stage. Use one positive direction for the whole journey.

At a smooth boundary, the final velocity of stage 1 becomes the initial velocity of stage 2. Write v₁ = u₂ before choosing equations. Time and displacement do not automatically reset in the story, but each stage may use its own duration and displacement.

figure.purpose: Show exactly which quantity crosses a stage boundary.
figure.brief: Two hand-written u-v-a-s-t tables joined by an arrow from v in table 1 to u in table 2.
figure.alt_text: Two variable tables for consecutive stages, connected from final velocity of the first to initial velocity of the second.

blocks.title: The same three tools, used in a chain
body: These are formulas to remember. Each applies only inside a straight-line interval with constant acceleration.
Here u is initial velocity in m s⁻¹, v is final velocity in m s⁻¹, a is acceleration in m s⁻², t is time in s and s is displacement in m.
Choose an equation for stage 1, calculate the boundary value, then treat that value as known in stage 2.

figure.purpose: Turn a multi-stage calculation into a visible information chain.
figure.brief: Flow diagram: stage 1 knowns to equation to boundary speed to stage 2 knowns to equation to final result.
figure.alt_text: A calculation flow carrying a boundary speed from the first stage into the second stage.

blocks.title: Carry the speed forward
body: A trolley starts at 2.0 m s⁻¹ and accelerates at 1.5 m s⁻² for 4.0 s. It then accelerates at -2.0 m s⁻² for 3.0 s.
Stage 1: v₁ = u₁ + a₁t₁ = 2.0 + 1.5 × 4.0 = 8.0 m s⁻¹.
Boundary: u₂ = v₁ = 8.0 m s⁻¹.
The cart still moves in the positive direction. Its positive velocity has become smaller.

figure.purpose: Model a complete forward two-stage layout with signs and units.
figure.brief: Annotated worked layout in two boxes with the 8.0 m s^-1 boundary value highlighted once and reused.
figure.alt_text: Two boxed calculations showing a trolley reaching 8.0 metres per second, then slowing to 2.0 metres per second.

blocks.title: The second stage does not start from rest
body: It can feel natural to write u₂ = 0 because the clock for stage 2 starts at zero. That mixes up resetting time with resetting motion.
The clock label may restart for convenience, but velocity changes continuously unless the story says there is an impact or stop. Carry v₁ into u₂. A quick motion sketch exposes the mistake.

figure.purpose: Contrast a reset clock with a continuous velocity.
figure.brief: Split comparison: correct timeline keeps the velocity arrow across the boundary; mistaken timeline erases it when the stage clock resets.
figure.alt_text: A comparison showing that resetting the stage clock does not reset the cart's velocity.

blocks.title: Work backward from the state you know
body: Suppose a cart ends at 3.0 m s⁻¹ after accelerating at -1.0 m s⁻² for 5.0 s. The word final does not mean you must calculate forward.
Use v = u + at and solve for the earlier velocity: u = v - at = 3.0 - (-1.0 × 5.0) = 8.0 m s⁻¹.
Now that boundary velocity can become the final velocity of the previous stage. Reverse problems are ordinary equations with the known state placed at the later end.

figure.purpose: Show that information can flow backward while time still runs forward.
figure.brief: Timeline arrow points forward, calculation arrow points from known final state back to unknown boundary state.
figure.alt_text: A forward time arrow and a backward reasoning arrow between the final and boundary states.

blocks.title: Linked stages: accelerate, then brake
body: A tram starts from rest, accelerates at 1.5 m s^-2 for 8.0 s, then brakes at -2.0 m s^-2 until it stops.
Stage 1: v = u + at = 0 + (1.5)(8.0) = 12.0 m s^-1. This boundary value becomes the initial velocity of stage 2.
Stage 1 distance: s = ut + 1/2 at^2 = 48 m.
Total distance is 48 + 36 = 84 m. Check stage 2 by average velocity: ((12.0 + 0)/2)(6.0) = 36 m.

figure.purpose: Make the reasoning in linked stages: accelerate, then brake visible.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch summary with a positive axis, compact values, arrows, and only the labels needed for the reasoning.
figure.alt_text: Teacher sketch for linked stages: accelerate, then brake.

blocks.title: Reverse solve from the final boundary
body: A shuttle finishes a 30 m stage at 14 m s^-1 after accelerating at 2.0 m s^-2. Find the speed at the start of that stage.
The final boundary is known: v = 14 m s^-1. Also a = +2.0 m s^-2 and s = +30 m.
The speed at the earlier boundary is u = sqrt(76) = 8.72 m s^-1. We take the positive root because the shuttle is stated to move forward.

figure.purpose: Make the reasoning in reverse solve from the final boundary visible.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn teacher-sketch summary with a positive axis, compact values, arrows, and only the labels needed for the reasoning.
figure.alt_text: Teacher sketch for reverse solve from the final boundary.

blocks.title: Split, link, solve and check
body: First split wherever acceleration changes. Second label each stage with signed u, v, a, s and t. Third write the boundary link. Fourth solve the stage that has enough information, even if that means working backward. Fifth carry the result and solve the next stage.

Sometimes two routes are possible. For example, total displacement can be found by adding stage displacements, while an endpoint may also be checked with a different registered equation inside its own stage. Agreement is evidence that the boundary and signs were handled correctly.
The opening cart needs two models joined by one shared velocity. That is the new picture: a long journey is a chain of valid short models, not one oversized equation.

concepts_taught: A change in acceleration creates a new constant-acceleration stage.
A continuous boundary velocity links adjacent stages.
Known later states can be used to reason backward.
Alternative valid routes can check an intermediate or final result.
misconceptions_addressed: One equation can cover intervals with different accelerations.
Resetting a stage clock resets velocity.
A calculation must always proceed from the beginning of the story.
skills_students_can_now_use: Split a journey into constant-acceleration stages.
Work backward from a final state.
Compare routes and delay rounding until the final answer.
reverse solve from the final boundary
next_lesson_can_assume: Students can solve linked horizontal constant-acceleration stages and use intermediate values consistently.
Students can work forward or backward with the three registered equations.
Students can keep one sign convention across a journey.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Students can choose vertical signs for free fall.
